analysis.one_liner: Bans the production, sale, and use of the herbicide atrazine nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban atrazine never received a committee hearing or vote, and the herbicide remains in use at roughly 80 million pounds a year.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would immediately and permanently cancel every registration for atrazine, the second-most-used herbicide in the United States, making it illegal to use, produce, sell, import, or export it [S2]. The bill's findings cite evidence that atrazine persists in water for decades, is among the most commonly detected pesticides in American drinking water, and is linked in the scientific literature to elevated cancer risks, birth defects, and reproductive harms [S2]. The ban would take effect by operation of law on the day of enactment, with food residue tolerances revoked within six months and no emergency-use exceptions [S2]. The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced, passed to a subcommittee three weeks later, and died there when the Congress ended [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Farmworkers and rural residents with the heaviest atrazine exposure, plus anyone who drinks water drawn from farm country streams and groundwater, where a USGS study found atrazine in about 75 percent of stream-water samples and 40 percent of groundwater samples from agricultural areas [S2]. Wildlife also gains: EPA's 2022 finding cited in the bill says atrazine is likely to adversely affect 1,013 threatened and endangered species — 56 percent of all listed plants and animals [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Immediately cancels all atrazine registrations and bans sale of existing stocks, ending new releases of a chemical that can persist in water for decades — atrazine was still detectable in European groundwater more than two decades after the EU banned it in 2003 [S2].

Removes a pesticide the bill's findings link to elevated cancer risk, birth defects, and reduced sperm count in the farmworker and rural populations most exposed, and which has been detected in rainwater, fog, ambient air, and drinking water sources nationwide [S2].

Cites USDA analysis that a ban would cut corn yields by only 1.19 percent, and a 2007 study finding no corn-yield decline in Germany or Italy after their 1991 ban, arguing the crop cost of losing atrazine is small [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The manufacturer and sellers of atrazine lose their product's registration outright, and corn and sorghum growers who rely on it as a low-cost, widely used herbicide would have to switch to alternatives, with USDA estimating a 1.19 percent corn yield decrease and some increase in weed-control costs [S2]. Because cancellation is immediate with no phase-out, growers would bear the transition abruptly [S2].

drawbacks.text: The ban is immediate and total: registrations are canceled by operation of law on enactment, existing stocks cannot be sold or used, and no emergency-use exception is allowed, giving farmers no transition period to arrange substitute weed control [S2].

Farmers lose their second-most-used herbicide, and even with USDA's low 1.19 percent yield estimate for corn, any yield loss and alternative-herbicide costs fall on growers and ultimately on food prices [S2].

A blanket statutory ban removes the issue from EPA's regular scientific review process, where atrazine is currently registered under federal limits; some would argue for tighter regulation through that process rather than outright prohibition (general policy point; the provided sources do not include EPA's position on this bill).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential public-health and environmental gain is large and the cited crop cost is small — a 1.19 percent corn yield decrease, with European precedent suggesting even that may overstate it [S2]. The main honest criticism is design, not direction: an instant, no-exceptions cancellation leaves growers no runway to switch herbicides in a single season. On balance the bill's cost falls on a narrow set of producers while the benefit — less atrazine in drinking water and in the bodies of farmworkers and rural residents — is broad.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Agriculture Committee and one of its subcommittees from October 2024 until the Congress ended in early January 2025, and never got a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the Ban Atrazine Toxicants Act on October 11, 2024, joined by Reps. McGovern, Norton, and Adams [S1][S4].

The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture, the committee with jurisdiction over pesticides, and on November 4, 2024 was referred further to its Subcommittee on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology [S4].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — was ever taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died without a vote [S1][S4].

Had it passed, the bill would have deemed atrazine to cause unreasonable adverse effects to humans and permanently canceled all its registrations by operation of law, bypassing ordinary cancellation proceedings under federal pesticide law [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Atrazine's manufacturer and the growers who use it are better off, because the herbicide stays on the market at roughly 80 million pounds a year, while the populations with the heaviest exposure continue to bear it [S2].

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban all atrazine use, production, sale, importation, and exportation [S1][S2].

for.name: Reps. Jim McGovern, Eleanor Holmes Norton, and Alma Adams
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsors at introduction; no other members signed on during the bill's 84-day life [S3].

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from its October 11, 2024 referral through the end of the Congress without any hearing or markup, then referred it to a subcommittee, where it died [S4].

against.name: Rep. Glenn Thompson
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never brought the bill to a markup or hearing before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters — the sponsor and three cosponsors — were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Agriculture Committee never acted on the bill; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Atrazine manufacturers and distributors (led by Syngenta)
industries.note: An immediate, permanent cancellation of all registrations wipes out the US market for the country's second-most-used herbicide, about 80 million pounds a year [S2]. The industry's interest in keeping atrazine registered runs against the public's interest in less atrazine in drinking water and in the bodies of farmworkers and rural residents [S2].

Growers lose a cheap, widely used weed killer and, per USDA figures cited in the bill, would absorb a 1.19 percent corn yield decrease plus the cost of switching herbicides [S2]. Rural growers and their communities are also among the populations most exposed to atrazine's health effects, so they sit on both sides of the ledger [S2].

industries.industry: Turf, golf course, and rights-of-way vegetation managers
industries.note: These users lose access to atrazine for weed control and would need substitutes; the bill's ban covers all uses of the pesticide [S2].
